title_original: A Selection of Photobooks, by Bill Shapiro
excerpt_original: Bill Shapiro, former editor-in-chief of LIFE, picks the new photobooks worth your time. Today’s selection: a reassessment of Walker Evans, four decades of Steve McCurry, and Chris Killip’s North of England. L’article A Selection of Photobooks, by Bill Shapiro est apparu en…

blocks.text: Walker Evans: Now and Then , by David Campany

I’ve now had a good, long look at Walker Evans: Now and Then , a sweeping new book that goes wide and deep on his work and begins with a quote, from Evans, that I love: “Stare. It is the way to educate the eye, and something more. Stare, pry, listen, eavesdrop. Die knowing something. You are not here long.”

Paging through Now and Then , it becomes incredibly clear that the ghost of Walker Evans is everywhere and has been for a long time. In fact, many of the pictures in this book look quite familiar, and I’m not talking about the ones we’ve all seen before. Why is that? Because the number of photographers Evans has influenced and continues to influence (whether they know it or not) is absolutely staggering. The evidence is right here: as clear in his subway pictures as it is in his vernacular signage.

blocks.alt: Two older women in hats and coats seated side by side in a New York subway car
blocks.caption: [Subway Passengers, New York], 1938 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.alt: Close-up of a torn, peeling movie poster showing two painted women's faces and the letters SA
blocks.caption: Torn Movie Poster (Truro, Massachusetts), 1931 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.alt: Blurred illuminated theater marquees at night on Broadway advertising The Big House, Loew's and Lucky Strike
blocks.caption: Broadway, 1930 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.alt: A photo studio window display covered with dozens of small portrait prints behind large block letters spelling STUDIO
blocks.caption: Penny Picture Display, Savannah, 1936 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.text: The book is edited by David Campany, the creative director at the International Center of Photography, which has bloomed bright once again under his curatorial guidance. Campany has previously written about Evans in at least two books that I know of, so, like, the man knows of what he speaks.

A self-described “reassessment,” the book spans Evans’ career, from his surprising color Polaroids from the 1970s (which I’d never seen… or heard of) to his early work from the 1920s, from Fortune magazine stories (including a quirky take on shop sidewalk displays, a gleaming look at common tools, and color pictures of railroad insignias) to African sculpture (a commission from MoMA) to portraits to architecture to his well-known vernacular signs to what we now casually call “street photography.” His curiosity was relentless, his reach immense.

blocks.alt: A woman in a cloche hat and large fur collar stands on a New York street under an elevated railway, with cars behind her
blocks.caption: 42nd Street, 1929 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.alt: A woman stands in the doorway of a New Orleans barber shop painted with bold diagonal stripes, a striped barber pole in front
blocks.caption: Sidewalk and Shopfront, New Orleans, 1935 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.alt: The photographer's shadow in profile cast on a grey wall
blocks.caption: [Shadow Self-portrait, Juan-les-Pins, France], 1927 © Walker Evans Archive, The Metropolitan Museum of Art

blocks.text: The 320-page book is published by Thames & Hudson, and if you like to stare, well, then this book is for you.
Walker Evans: Now and Then , by David Campany is published by Thames & Hudson and available for $65.
The Haunted Eye , by Steve McCurry

Let’s take a look at one beautiful new photo book: The Haunted Eye by Steve McCurry. But before we get to the book itself, it is positively head-spinning to imagine everything Steve has seen over the course of his career. Now 76, McCurry made his name in his 20s when he embedded with the Mujahideen in Afghanistan; with his film sewn into his clothes, he snuck out of the country and delivered the first images of the Soviet invasion to the world.

Since then, he’s won truckloads of awards for his documentary pictures that double as fine art, and made what is widely considered one of the most recognizable portraits to grace a magazine cover: in 1984, he photographed Sharbat Gula, a girl with unforgettable eyes, living in a refugee camp. The picture, often referred to as “Afghan Girl,” ran on the cover of National Geographic in 1985. Steve, a man who covered the brutal impact of war upon the innocents in conflict zones all over the world, joined Magnum the following year.

blocks.alt: A line of armed soldiers walks across deep snow past a wooden church, a misty village on the slope behind
blocks.caption: Kashmir © Steve McCurry

blocks.text: McCurry’s new book dazzles. In 188 pages, it covers 40-plus years of pictures, many not previously published. And the colors. Sweet Lord, the colors! But this book also provides color in another way: in tightly written, evocative, short passages, Steve summons the precise moments when various photographs were made. Like this: “I remember the air inside that car feeling incredibly heavy, as if the space itself were shrinking around us. We were in Thai Nguyen Province, Viêt Nam, in 2007. I was there with Luong Van Tuyen in the moment her world fractured, the exact moment she was told she was HIV-positive. I watched through my lens as a single tear tracked down her cheek, a small, shimmering line of absolute shock.”

blocks.alt: A railway station at sunset with red train carriages and a steam locomotive, a domed mosque rising behind the platforms
blocks.caption: India © Steve McCurry

blocks.alt: A bright red and orange crab on black volcanic rock among dark marine iguanas and their tails
blocks.caption: Ecuador © Steve McCurry

blocks.text: The Haunted Eye , by Steve McCurry is published by Atelier EXB and available for €49.
Chris Killip: North , by Chris Killip
Now for the newest book from one of the world’s great photographers, Chris Killip, a documentarian preternaturally adept at finding the emotions buried within a moment.

Killip left school at 16, trained in hotel management, then became a photographer, then became an extraordinary photographer, then became such an extraordinary photographer that Harvard offered him a professorship. He died in 2020, at 74.

blocks.alt: An adult and a small child lean into the doorway of the Raby General Discount Store, its shutters chained open and covered in graffiti
blocks.caption: Raby Street store, Byker, Tyneside, 1975 © Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos

blocks.text: The pictures in this new book, Chris Killip: North , were made, yes, in the North, specifically the Northeast of England and Ireland, between 1975 and 1986. Those were hard years for the shipbuilders, rock-shovelers, and small-boat fishermen who populate Killip’s photographs. His pictures are bleak as ash but filled with a tenderness that’ll break your heart. And yet they’re never sappy, not even the images of children making the best of it as they sit barefoot on the sidewalk as a baby crawls toward an open front door. In fact, some of his pictures deliver an emotional wallop, but when I look at the image, I can’t pinpoint what, exactly, is making me feel that way.

blocks.alt: A boy swings on a rope in a brick doorway above two children holding a kitten, while two boys sit nearby covering their faces with their hands
blocks.caption: Byker, Tyneside, 1976 © Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos

blocks.alt: A younger man pushes an older man with a walking stick up a misty, rocky mountain slope
blocks.caption: Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo, Ireland, 1993–2005 © Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos

blocks.alt: A bearded man with thick curly hair rests his cheek against the head of a horse with a white blaze
blocks.caption: Seacoal beach, Lynemouth, Northumberland, 1983 © Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos

blocks.text: At 300-plus pages, North , published by Thames & Hudson, is a beefy book, and nearly half of its 224 images have never been published before; some of the rest are among Killip’s finest. The extremely knowledgeable Brad Feuerhelm (Ordinary Light on Instagram) beat me to the review, and his post features some fantastic pages from the book, so check it out.
Chris Killip: North , by Chris Killip is published by Thames & Hudson and available for $95.

blocks.alt: A young punk in bleached trousers and boots sits on a bench rolling a cigarette while another young man crouches against a brick wall
blocks.caption: Whippet and Richard, Skinningrove, North Yorkshire, 1982 © Chris Killip Photography Trust / Magnum Photos
